What a Bernoulli shift is

Choose a finite alphabet A with probability vector p. A point of A^ℤ is a bi-infinite sequence, sampled with independent p-distributed coordinates. The transformation T shifts each coordinate one place: (Tx)ₙ = xₙ₊₁.

The entropy of this Bernoulli system is H(p) = −Σₐ pₐ log₂ pₐ. Entropy was already known to be invariant under measure-preserving isomorphism. Ornstein's theorem proves the difficult converse within the Bernoulli class: equal base entropy implies isomorphism. [1]

Thus different alphabets and probability vectors can describe equivalent shift systems. The isomorphism is measurable, defined up to null sets, and intertwines the shifts. It is not asserted to be a topological conjugacy or a one-symbol recoding.
Why the converse was difficult

Entropy compresses a process into one asymptotic information rate. At first it provides only a necessary test: unequal values rule out isomorphism. A complete invariant requires a construction or existence argument in the opposite direction.

Ornstein's machinery compares long finite blocks and increasingly accurate joinings and recodings. The important step is not simply observing that typical blocks have comparable counts. It is making successive approximations consistent enough to obtain an invertible measurable map on the infinite processes.
This is why the theorem is stronger than a counting calculation. It upgrades controlled finite approximations to an exact equivalence modulo null sets. [1,2]
The d-bar viewpoint

For stationary processes on a common finite alphabet, let λ range over stationary couplings with the required marginal laws. Define d-bar as the infimum of the probability of a mismatch at coordinate zero.
This compares whole processes through compatible joint distributions, not independent one-coordinate comparisons. Stationarity makes the mismatch probability representative of the mismatch rate.

The d-bar framework is one of the tools of Ornstein theory. Equal entropy does not imply d-bar distance zero between arbitrary original codings. Recoding and the special structural properties of Bernoulli processes are essential. [2]
The structural hypothesis is indispensable

Entropy does not classify arbitrary measure-preserving systems. A simple warning comes from finite probability spaces: the identity map and a nontrivial cyclic permutation both have zero entropy but are not isomorphic as transformations.

The Bernoulli theorem is therefore not an instruction to search for a single number and ignore structure. Its force comes from identifying a class where enough randomness is present to support a very strong classification argument.

A necessary invariant, a complete invariant on one class, and a universal classification are three different achievements. Ornstein established the middle one in a major and initially unexpected setting.
From ℤ to amenable groups

For a countable amenable group, Følner sets have small relative boundary under each fixed translation. Ornstein and Weiss used finite towers and quasi-tiling ideas to extend approximation, entropy and isomorphism theory from ℤ-actions to amenable-group actions. [3]

An informal picture is an infinite action approximated by many large finite pieces, with boundary errors controlled in measure. The precise action, freeness and measure assumptions must be retained; this is not a purely combinatorial tiling assertion.
The result connects classification with the same finite-versus-infinite theme that occurs in graph decompositions and local limits, while remaining a theorem in measured dynamics.
A later continuation beyond amenability

Seward proved that Bernoulli shifts over any countably infinite group with equal base Shannon entropy are isomorphic, extending Ornstein's sufficiency theorem beyond the amenable case. The paper builds on work of Lewis Bowen and also treats finitary isomorphisms for finite bases. [4]
The statement here is equal entropy implies isomorphism. It should not silently be strengthened to a complete two-way entropy classification for arbitrary countable groups.

The broader methodological lesson is to separate the invariant, the structural class and the equivalence relation. Only after these are specified can approximate finite information be asked to determine an infinite object.

An original MAX-CUT example: filled and hollow vertices define the two sides. Four edges cross; the fifth stays on one side. An odd cycle cannot alternate all the way around.

An original worked example: 000 becomes 010 after one bit flips; majority decoding recovers 000. This is a repetition code, not the seven-bit Hamming code.

Splaying 10 in the three-key tree uses a zig-zig: first rotate 20 above 30, then 10 above 20. Key order is preserved; the next access to 10 starts at the root.

A data structure is a representation together with operations and guarantees. Ask what must stay true after an update, which operations are frequent, and what counts as expensive.
